source_text: Pars igitur et voluptati consulens et pavori, vel arenae, vel circi, vel scenae populis comitata luxuria, ambiens in omnibus flagitiis obtendere necessitatem, qua commissi invidia semper levatur, et fragores saeculi praevaricatione vitare; ea ergo sunt, quae comitatiorem faciunt vitiorum defensionem. Ex quo tamen vulgo pars maxima, ut praefatus sum, Traducianis et Catholicis vel de Deo rationes credidit consonare.
pass_a_gloss: A part therefore consulting both pleasure and fear, luxury accompanied by the peoples either of the sand or of the circus or of the stage, canvassing in all outrages to hold out a necessity by which the spite of what was committed is always lightened, and to avoid the crashes of the age by prevarication; those therefore are the things which make the defense of vices more accompanied. From which crowd nevertheless the greatest part, as I said in the preface, believed the reasons of the Traducians and of the Catholics even about God to agree.

lemmas.lexica: Julian's polemic label for teachers of tradux peccati
LS tradux=vine-shoot/layer; Blaise tradux peccati=transmission of sin by descent
LS necessitas; Blaise vs free choice
LS ratio; Blaise use of reason required for sin

pass_b_english: Thus one group caters both to pleasure and to fear. Its indulgence travels with the crowds of the arena, circus, or theater, seeking to excuse every disgrace by necessity, which always lightens the blame for what was done, and to avoid the world’s uproar by abandoning its principles. These are the things that win a larger following for the defense of vices. Yet most of that crowd, as I said before, believed that advocates of inherited sin and catholics agreed at least in their account of God.

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Julian contrasts opportunity/help with imposed necessity; load-bearing against natural compulsion to sin.
For Julian, sin requires rational choice; infants lack usus rationis.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
